ADE-001.e: Lower rates raise investment and equilibrium output.
o: Interest rate–output combinations where the goods market clears; downward sloping
ADE-001.x:
Basis: Hicks (1937), Hansen (1953) – the IS–LM model.
Analysis: The IS curve (Investment = Saving): (r, Y) combinations where the goods market clears (Y = C + I(r) + G). It slopes down: lower rates → more investment → higher demand and equilibrium output (via the multiplier).
Distractors: B is the LM curve (ADE-002); C is the Phillips curve; D is the BP curve in open models.

ADE-002.e: Higher output raises transactions demand for money, requiring a higher rate to clear.
o: Interest rate–output combinations where real money supply equals demand; upward sloping
ADE-002.x:
Basis: Hicks–Hansen (money market: M/P = L(Y, r)).
Analysis: The LM curve (Liquidity = Money): (r, Y) combinations where real money supply = real money demand. It slopes up: higher output → more transactions demand → with fixed money supply, rates must rise to cut speculative demand and restore balance.
Distractors: B is IS; C and D aren't in basic IS–LM.

ADE-003.q: In the closed-economy IS–LM model, fiscal expansion causes:
ADE-003.e: Higher rates partly crowd out private investment.
o: IS shifts right: output and interest rate rise
LM shifts right: output rises, rate falls
ADE-003.x:
Basis: IS–LM model.
Analysis: Higher G or lower taxes → IS shifts right → new equilibrium: higher output and higher rates (along an upward LM). Higher rates curb private investment – partial crowding out (ADE-008) → output rises less than the simple Keynesian multiplier.
Distractors: B describes monetary expansion (ADE-004); C and D have the wrong direction.

ADE-004.q: In IS–LM, a money supply increase causes:
o: LM shifts right: output rises, rate falls
ADE-004.x:
Basis: IS–LM model.
Analysis: More money (higher M/P) → LM shifts right → lower rates → more investment → higher output (along a downward IS). It works best with a flat IS (rate-sensitive investment) and a non-flat LM (no liquidity trap – ADE-014).
Distractors: B – IS shifts with fiscal policy; C is the reverse; D – IS–LM assumes fixed short-run prices, saying nothing of falling inflation.

ADE-005.q: IS: Y = 1,000 − 50r; LM: Y = 600 + 50r (r in %). What is the equilibrium interest rate (%)?
ADE-005.x:
Basis: IS–LM model (solving the system).
Working: IS = LM: 1,000 − 50r = 600 + 50r → 400 = 100r → r = 4%.
Check: Y_IS = 1,000 − 200 = 800; Y_LM = 600 + 200 = 800 ✓.

ADE-006.q: IS: Y = 1,000 − 50r; LM: Y = 600 + 50r (r in %). What is equilibrium output?
ADE-006.x:
Basis: IS–LM model.
Working: Substitute r = 4 into IS: Y = 1,000 − 50 × 4 = 800; LM check: 600 + 50 × 4 = 800 ✓.
Analysis: (r = 4%, Y = 800) is simultaneous goods- and money-market equilibrium – the starting point for policy analysis (ADE-007, ADE-008).

ADE-007.q: Higher government spending shifts IS to Y = 1,100 − 50r (LM stays Y = 600 + 50r). What is new equilibrium output?
ADE-007.x:
Basis: IS–LM model (fiscal expansion).
Working: 1,100 − 50r = 600 + 50r → 500 = 100r → r = 5%; Y = 1,100 − 250 = 850 (LM check: 600 + 250 = 850 ✓).
Analysis: IS shifts right by 100, but output rises only 50 (800 → 850) and rates by 1 point – the gap is crowding out (ADE-008).

ADE-008.q: Initially IS: Y = 1,000 − 50r and LM: Y = 600 + 50r (r = 4%, Y = 800). Higher government spending shifts IS to Y = 1,100 − 50r, new equilibrium r = 5%, Y = 850. At a fixed 4% rate output would rise by 100. How much output is crowded out by the higher rate?
ADE-008.e: Horizontal IS shift = 100; actual rise 50 → 50 crowded out.
ADE-008.x:
Basis: IS–LM model (crowding out).
Working: Holding r at 4%: Y = 1,100 − 200 = 900 (+100 = the horizontal IS shift). Actually Y = 850 (+50). Crowding out = 100 − 50 = 50 units of output.
Analysis: The rate rise from 4% to 5% cuts investment by 50 → half the stimulus is offset. The central bank can accommodate (expanding money to hold rates) to avoid crowding out – policy coordination.

ADE-009.q: When LM is steep (money demand insensitive to rates), fiscal policy is less effective due to strong crowding out.
ADE-009.e: True. In the extreme vertical-LM case, crowding out is complete.
ADE-009.x:
Basis: IS–LM model (LM slope and fiscal effectiveness).
Analysis: True. A steep LM means money demand is rate-insensitive → fiscal expansion drives rates up sharply → large crowding out → weak fiscal policy. At the extreme, a vertical LM (classical/monetarist view) means full crowding out with no output change. Conversely, a flat LM (liquidity trap) means none (ADE-014).

ADE-010.q: Mundell–Fleming, floating rate, perfect capital mobility, small economy: fiscal expansion will:
ADE-010.e: Monetary policy is the effective tool under this regime.
o: Barely raise output as currency appreciation cuts net exports equivalently
ADE-010.x:
Basis: Mundell (1963), Fleming (1962) – small open economy, perfect capital mobility.
Analysis: Floating rates: fiscal expansion → upward rate pressure → capital inflows → currency appreciation → net exports fall, cancelling the demand boost → output barely changes (crowding out via the exchange rate). Rates are pinned to world rates. Monetary policy is the effective tool (via the exchange-rate channel).
Distractors: B is wrong; C – the currency appreciates; D – domestic rates stay at world levels.

ADE-011.q: Mundell–Fleming, fixed rate, perfect capital mobility: independent monetary policy is:
ADE-011.e: Fiscal policy is effective under this regime.
o: Ineffective – the central bank must intervene to hold the peg and money supply reverts
ADE-011.x:
Basis: Mundell–Fleming (fixed rate, free capital).
Analysis: The central bank expands money → rates tend to fall → capital flows out, depreciation pressure → to hold the peg it must sell FX and absorb local currency → money returns to its old level → independent monetary policy fails. Fiscal policy works here (the central bank must inject money to defend the peg – automatic accommodation).
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note: A manifestation of the trilemma (MCR-080, ADE-012).

ADE-012.q: Under a fixed rate with free capital, money supply becomes endogenous as the central bank buys/sells FX to hold the peg.
ADE-012.e: True. It's the impossible trinity at work.
ADE-012.x:
Basis: Mundell–Fleming; the trilemma.
Analysis: True. Holding a peg with free capital forces the central bank to buy/sell FX on demand → each FX purchase injects local currency, each sale withdraws it → money supply is set by the balance of payments (endogenous), and the central bank loses control. Sterilisation (MCR-088) only softens this temporarily.

ADE-013.q: Select ALL factors that shift IS to the right:
ADE-013.x:
Basis: IS–LM model.
Analysis: IS shifts right when autonomous spending rises at every rate: (A) higher G; (B) lower taxes (more disposable income, higher C); (C) stronger business confidence – more autonomous investment; (D) higher autonomous exports.
Distractors: (E) Money supply shifts LM, not IS (ADE-004).

ADE-014.q: In a liquidity trap LM is flat at very low rates. Then:
ADE-014.e: It supports fiscal stimulus at the lower bound.
o: Monetary policy is largely ineffective; fiscal policy works without crowding out
ADE-014.x:
Basis: Keynes (1936); Krugman (1998) – liquidity trap in IS–LM.
Analysis: A flat LM at the rate floor: more money merely extends LM horizontally without cutting rates → monetary policy barely works (MCR-039). Fiscal expansion moves IS along the flat section → output rises by the full multiplier with no rate rise → no crowding out.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note: The argument for fiscal stimulus in the US, Europe and Japan after 2008 and 2020.

ADE-015.q: Real money demand L = 0.5Y − 100r; real money supply 300 → LM: Y = 600 + 200r. IS: Y = 1,200 − 100r. What is equilibrium output?

ADE-016.q: The AD curve can be derived from IS–LM by varying the price level (changing real money balances).
ADE-016.e: True. A higher price level lowers M/P, shifts LM left and cuts output.
ADE-016.x:
Basis: IS–LM and AD–AS (Mankiw – Macroeconomics).
Analysis: True. With fixed nominal M, a higher price level P → lower real money M/P → LM shifts left → higher rates, lower equilibrium output. The set of such (P, Y) pairs forms a downward-sloping AD. Fiscal and monetary moves shifting IS/LM shift AD accordingly.

ADE-017.q: Rational expectations differ from adaptive expectations in that they:
ADE-017.e: Rational expectations have no systematic errors but still have random ones.
o: Use all available information, including expected policy, not just past values
Look only at last year's inflation
ADE-017.x:
Basis: Muth (1961) – rational expectations; Lucas (1972); Cagan (1956) – adaptive expectations.
Analysis: Adaptive expectations rely on past values, adjusting gradually to errors (πᵉ = last year's π). Rational expectations use all available information, including economic models and expected policy → no systematic errors (right on average) but still random errors from surprises.
Distractors: B describes adaptive expectations; C – not always correct; D is wrong.
Note (markets): asset prices embed expectations – news already 'priced in' moves prices little on release.

o: Parameters estimated from past data may shift when policy changes, because behaviour and expectations change
ADE-018.x:
Basis: Lucas (1976), 'Econometric Policy Evaluation: A Critique'.
Analysis: Parameters estimated from past data reflect behaviour under the old policy regime; when policy changes, expectations and behaviour change → parameters shift → forecasts of new-policy effects using old models may fail. It spurred micro-founded models (DSGE) with 'deep' parameters (preferences, technology).
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note (investment systems): trading rules optimised on one regime (low rates, QE) can fail when regimes change – one reason to test robustness across regimes.

ADE-019.q: Per Kydland–Prescott, discretionary policy can cause 'inflation bias' due to time inconsistency.
ADE-019.e: True. Policymakers are tempted to create surprise inflation once expectations are set; the public anticipates this.
ADE-019.x:
Basis: Kydland & Prescott (1977), 'Rules Rather than Discretion'; Barro & Gordon (1983).
Analysis: True. Time inconsistency: the central bank promises low inflation; once expectations and wages are set, it's tempted to surprise with inflation to lift output. Rational people anticipate this → expect high inflation from the start → equilibrium: higher inflation with no extra output – inflation bias. Remedies: commitment, rules, independence (ADE-020).

ADE-020.q: Commitment devices that reduce time inconsistency include:
ADE-020.e: Credible commitment keeps inflation expectations low and stable.
o: Central bank independence, public inflation targets, policy rules
ADE-020.x:
Basis: Advanced macroeconomics (Rogoff 1985 – the 'conservative' central banker; Walsh 1995 – central bank contracts).
Analysis: Commitment devices: central bank independence (delegating to someone more price-stability-minded – Rogoff), publicly accountable inflation targets, policy rules (Taylor – ADE-021) → less motive and scope for surprise inflation → low, stable expectations.
Distractors: B and C destroy credibility; D – money-financed deficits cause inflation (fiscal dominance – ADE-029).

ADE-021.q: Taylor rule: i = r* + π + 0.5(π − π*) + 0.5 × output gap. With r* = 2%, π = 5%, π* = 3%, gap −2%. What policy rate is implied (%)?
ADE-021.x:
Basis: Taylor (1993).
Working: i = 2 + 5 + 0.5 × (5 − 3) + 0.5 × (−2) = 2 + 5 + 1 − 1 = 7%.
Analysis: Inflation 2 points above target pushes up, a −2% output gap pulls down – offsetting, leaving a real rate of 7 − 5 = 2% = r* (neutral). Application: compare actual policy rates with the Taylor rule to judge whether policy is loose or tight.

ADE-022.q: Taylor rule: i = r* + π + 0.5(π − π*) + 0.5 × output gap. With r* = 2%, π = 2%, π* = 3%, gap −4%. What policy rate is implied (%)?
ADE-022.x:
Basis: Taylor (1993).
Working: i = 2 + 2 + 0.5 × (2 − 3) + 0.5 × (−4) = 4 − 0.5 − 2 = 1.5%.
Analysis: Below-target inflation and a deep negative gap → a low suggested rate and a real rate of 1.5 − 2 = −0.5% (easing). If the rule implied a negative rate (deeper recession), the zero lower bound binds → QE and forward guidance (ADE-023).

ADE-023.q: Forward guidance affects long rates via expectations of the short-rate path.
ADE-023.e: True. Effectiveness depends on central bank credibility.
ADE-023.x:
Basis: Advanced macroeconomics (Eggertsson & Woodford 2003; Campbell et al. 2012 – Delphic vs Odyssean guidance).
Analysis: True. Long rates ≈ average expected future short rates + a term premium. Forward guidance ('rates low at least until…') shifts expected rate paths → long rates fall even with short rates at the floor. Effectiveness depends on credibility (ADE-028).
Note: Investors should track central bank messaging (Fed, SBV) – expectation shifts move valuations before rates actually change.

ADE-024.e: When u = uₙ, inflation equals expected inflation.
o: π = πᵉ − β(u − uₙ) + supply shock
ADE-024.x:
Basis: Friedman (1968), Phelps (1967) – expectations-augmented Phillips curve.
Analysis: π = πᵉ − β(u − uₙ) + ε: inflation = expected inflation − β × cyclical unemployment + supply shock. At u = uₙ (no shock), π = πᵉ. Unemployment below the natural rate → inflation above expectations (ADE-025). In the long run πᵉ adjusts → a vertical long-run Phillips curve (MCR-021).
Distractors: B omits expectations; C holds only in the long run; D has the wrong sign.

ADE-025.q: π = πᵉ − 0.5(u − uₙ). With πᵉ = 4%, u = 3%, uₙ = 5%. What is inflation (%)?
ADE-025.x:
Basis: Expectations-augmented Phillips curve.
Working: π = 4 − 0.5 × (3 − 5) = 4 − 0.5 × (−2) = 4 + 1 = 5%.
Analysis: Unemployment 2 points below natural → inflation 1 point above expectations. If sustained, πᵉ rises to 5% → keeping u at 3% means accepting 6%, 7%… (accelerating inflation – the basis of NAIRU).

ADE-026.e: High credibility lowers the sacrifice ratio.
o: Cumulative percentage points of GDP lost to cut inflation by 1 point
ADE-026.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (Ball 1994 – sacrifice ratio).
Analysis: The sacrifice ratio = cumulative percentage points of GDP lost to cut inflation by 1 point – the cost of disinflation. Credible policy lets expectations adjust fast → a low ratio ('painless' disinflation); weak credibility → deeper recession (e.g., Volcker 1980–1982).
Distractors: B, C and D are other concepts.

ADE-027.q: The sacrifice ratio is 2. To cut inflation by 3 points, how much cumulative output is lost (% of GDP)?
ADE-027.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (sacrifice ratio).
Working: Total output lost = sacrifice ratio × points of disinflation = 2 × 3 = 6% of GDP (cumulative, e.g., 3 years × 2% a year).
Analysis: Disinflation can be fast (cold turkey – short, deep recession) or gradual (long, shallow); in simple models total cost is similar; credibility lowers the ratio (ADE-026).

ADE-028.q: Select ALL factors that raise central bank credibility:
o: A record of hitting inflation targets
Fiscal discipline, no monetary financing of deficits
ADE-028.x:
Basis: Advanced macroeconomics (Blinder 2000 – central bank credibility).
Analysis: Credibility rises with: (A) a record of hitting targets; (B) transparent, consistent communication; (C) legal and operational independence; (D) fiscal discipline – no money-financed deficits (avoiding fiscal dominance – ADE-029).
Distractors: (E) Arbitrary target changes unanchor expectations.

ADE-029.q: 'Fiscal dominance' can force a central bank to accept higher inflation to keep public debt service sustainable.
ADE-029.e: True. High public debt shrinks room for monetary tightening.
ADE-029.x:
Basis: Sargent & Wallace (1981), 'Some Unpleasant Monetarist Arithmetic'.
Analysis: True. With high public debt and unadjusting fiscal policy, the central bank may be forced to keep rates low or monetise deficits to sustain debt → accepting higher inflation; tightening today can make debt grow faster, raising inflation tomorrow. High debt narrows room to tighten.
Note (investing): fiscal-dominance risk in high-debt countries is a long-run inflation factor for valuing bonds and gold.

ADE-030.q: The 'policy ineffectiveness proposition' (Sargent–Wallace) says that with rational expectations and flexible prices:
ADE-030.e: New Keynesian models add sticky prices, so policy has short-run effects.
o: Anticipated monetary policy doesn't affect real output, only prices
ADE-030.x:
Basis: Sargent & Wallace (1975) – policy ineffectiveness proposition; Fischer (1977), Taylor (1980) – staggered contracts.
Analysis: With rational expectations and flexible prices and wages, anticipated monetary policy is already in expectations and prices adjust at once → no real output effect, only prices; only surprises matter. New Keynesian models add sticky prices and wages (contracts, menu costs) → anticipated policy still has short-run effects.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.

o: The agent's goals differ from the principal's and the agent's actions are hard to observe
ADE-031.x:
Basis: Jensen & Meckling (1976), 'Theory of the Firm'.
Analysis: Principal–agent problem: agents (managers, borrowers) have different goals from principals (shareholders, banks) and actions that are hard to observe (asymmetric information) → they may act for themselves (perks, empire building, excessive caution or risk). Agency costs = monitoring + bonding costs + residual loss.
Distractors: B and C involve no conflict; D is wrong.
Note (company analysis): assessing governance, capital allocation and executive pay tests agency costs.

ADE-032.q: The 'incentive compatibility' constraint in contract design requires:
ADE-032.e: The participation constraint ensures they accept the contract.
o: The agent voluntarily chooses the desired action because it's best for them
ADE-032.x:
Basis: Contract theory (Holmström 1979; Bolton & Dewatripont 2005).
Analysis: The incentive compatibility (IC) constraint: the contract makes the principal's desired action (high effort) also the agent's best choice – rewards for effort cover its cost. The participation constraint (ADE-033) ensures they sign.
Distractors: B is participation; C – fixed pay creates no incentive; D – full monitoring is usually infeasible.

ADE-033.e: Otherwise the agent rejects the contract.
o: The agent's expected utility from the contract is at least their best outside option
ADE-033.x:
Basis: Contract theory.
Analysis: The participation (individual rationality) constraint: the agent's expected utility from the contract ≥ their best outside option (market pay, another job) – otherwise they decline. An optimal principal usually makes it bind exactly, not overpaying.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the definition.

ADE-034.q: If the agent is risk-neutral and effort is unobservable, 'selling the firm' (agent pays a fixed fee and keeps all output) achieves the first best.
ADE-034.e: True. The agent bears all consequences and chooses optimal effort; with risk aversion there's a risk–incentive trade-off.
ADE-034.x:
Basis: Contract theory (Harris & Raviv 1979; Holmström 1979).
Analysis: True. With a risk-neutral agent and unobservable effort, 'selling the firm' (the agent pays a fixed fee and keeps all output) → the agent is the residual claimant bearing all consequences → chooses optimal effort at no risk-bearing cost. With a risk-averse agent, loading all risk on them is costly → a trade-off between risk sharing and incentives.
Note: It explains why owner-managers (or executives with large stakes) tend to be better aligned with shareholders.

ADE-035.q: Akerlof's 'market for lemons' shows asymmetric information can:
ADE-035.e: Warranties, independent inspection and dealer reputation are remedies.
o: Drive good cars out, leaving only lemons, even causing market collapse
ADE-035.x:
Basis: Akerlof (1970), 'The Market for Lemons' (Nobel 2001).
Analysis: Sellers know quality, buyers don't → buyers pay only for average quality → owners of good cars (worth more than average) withdraw → average quality falls → prices fall further → a spiral leaving only lemons, possibly market collapse (ADE-036). Solutions: warranties (signals), independent inspection, dealer reputation, disclosure rules.
Distractors: B, C and D contradict the result.
Note (capital markets): good firms valued too low may avoid IPOs/issuance → outsiders should be wary of issues at rich valuations.

ADE-036.q: Used cars: buyers value good cars at 200 and bad at 100; 50/50 mix; buyers can't tell them apart. Good-car sellers sell only at ≥ 180, bad at ≥ 80. What is the equilibrium price?
ADE-036.e: Buyers pay at most the expected 150 < 180 → good cars exit; only bad cars remain → price 100.
ADE-036.x:
Basis: Akerlof (1970).
Working: Buyers can't tell types → pay at most expected value = 0.5 × 200 + 0.5 × 100 = 150. Good-car sellers need ≥ 180 > 150 → they exit. Only lemons remain → buyers know it → pay at most 100 ≥ 80 (lemon sellers accept) → equilibrium price 100.
Analysis: Asymmetric information destroys all good-car trades even though buyers value them at 200 > the 180 sellers need – an efficiency loss.

ADE-037.q: In Spence's signalling model, education is a credible signal of ability when:
ADE-037.e: Differential costs create a separating equilibrium.
o: It's significantly cheaper for high-ability than low-ability people to obtain
ADE-037.x:
Basis: Spence (1973), 'Job Market Signaling' (Nobel 2001).
Analysis: Education credibly signals ability when its cost (fees, effort, time) is significantly lower for high-ability than low-ability people (single crossing) → the able study, the less able won't mimic → a separating equilibrium (ADE-038, ADE-039). It works even if education adds no productivity.
Distractors: B is human-capital theory; C – equal costs prevent separation; D is wrong.

ADE-038.q: High-ability productivity 200, low 100. Cost per year of schooling: high 40, low 80. Employers pay 200 if schooling ≥ e* years, else 100. What minimum e* stops low types mimicking?
ADE-038.x:
Basis: Spence (1973) – the low type's no-mimicking condition.
Working: Low types don't mimic if not studying pays at least as much: 100 ≥ 200 − 80e* → 80e* ≥ 100 → e* ≥ 1.25 years.
Analysis: At e* = 1.25 low types are indifferent (200 − 100 = 100); any lower e* and they study too to get 200 → the signal fails (pooling).

ADE-039.q: Signalling model: high-ability productivity 200, low 100; cost per year of schooling 40 for high, 80 for low; employers pay 200 if schooling ≥ e* years, else 100. What maximum e* still makes high types willing to signal?
ADE-039.e: High types: 200 − 40e* ≥ 100 → e* ≤ 2.5. Separating equilibria have 1.25 ≤ e* ≤ 2.5.
ADE-039.x:
Basis: Spence (1973) – the high type's participation condition.
Working: High types study if: 200 − 40e* ≥ 100 → 40e* ≤ 100 → e* ≤ 2.5 years. With ADE-038: separation for 1.25 ≤ e* ≤ 2.5.
Analysis: Any e* in the range is an equilibrium; e* = 1.25 is most efficient (cheapest signal – the Riley criterion). Signalling costs are a social loss if education adds no productivity.

ADE-040.q: Select ALL mechanisms banks use to limit borrower moral hazard:
ADE-040.e: Equity contribution gives the borrower 'skin in the game'.
o: Monitoring use of funds, periodic reporting
ADE-040.x:
Basis: Information economics (Holmström & Tirole 1997 – equity stakes; Smith & Warner 1979 – covenants).
Analysis: Curbing borrower moral hazard: (A) collateral – borrowers lose assets on default; (B) financial covenants (debt/EBITDA, DSCR) – limiting risky behaviour (AUD-009); (C) monitoring use of funds and periodic reporting; (D) equity contributions – 'skin in the game'.
Distractors: (E) Hiding loan terms worsens information asymmetry.

ADE-041.q: Efficiency wage theory says paying above market can raise productivity and reduce shirking but may cause involuntary unemployment.
ADE-041.x:
Basis: Shapiro & Stiglitz (1984), 'Equilibrium Unemployment as a Worker Discipline Device'.
Analysis: True. Firms can't perfectly monitor effort → paying above market makes job loss costly (less shirking), retains talent and lifts morale → higher productivity. When all firms do this, wages sit above equilibrium → labour supply exceeds demand → involuntary unemployment persists as a 'discipline device'.

ADE-042.q: Per Stiglitz–Weiss, banks may ration credit instead of raising rates because:
ADE-042.e: Adverse selection and moral hazard stop credit markets clearing through price.
o: Higher rates attract riskier borrowers and encourage riskier projects, lowering banks' expected returns
ADE-042.x:
Basis: Stiglitz & Weiss (1981), 'Credit Rationing in Markets with Imperfect Information'.
Analysis: High rates cause: (1) adverse selection – safe borrowers leave, risky ones (willing to pay because they may not repay) stay; (2) moral hazard – borrowers pick riskier projects to cover the rate. → Bank expected profit falls beyond a threshold rate → banks ration credit at the optimal rate instead of raising rates to clear the market.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note (Vietnam): small firms without collateral are often rationed despite willingness to pay high rates.

ADE-043.q: An insurer offers a low-premium/high-deductible plan and a high-premium/low-deductible plan. This is:
ADE-043.e: High-risk customers choose the low-deductible plan.
o: Screening via a contract menu so customers self-reveal risk
ADE-043.x:
Basis: Rothschild & Stiglitz (1976), 'Equilibrium in Competitive Insurance Markets'.
Analysis: A contract menu: low premium – high deductible (attracting low-risk buyers who rarely claim) and high premium – low deductible (attracting high-risk buyers) → customers reveal their risk through choice → screening (the uninformed party designs the mechanism), not signalling (initiated by the informed).
Distractors: B – signalling comes from the informed side; C – not individual pricing; D is wrong.

ADE-044.q: Per Jensen–Meckling, debt can reduce agency costs of equity because:
ADE-044.e: But excessive debt creates agency costs of debt (risk shifting to creditors).
o: Fixed repayments cut free cash flow that management could waste
ADE-044.x:
Basis: Jensen & Meckling (1976); Jensen (1986), 'Agency Costs of Free Cash Flow'.
Analysis: Abundant free cash flow lets managers waste it (negative-NPV projects, empire-building M&A, perks). Debt forces fixed principal and interest payments → less free cash under management control and more discipline, plus creditor monitoring. But excessive debt creates agency costs of debt: shareholders may gamble (shifting risk to creditors) or skip good projects (debt overhang).
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note: A reason to examine dividends and buybacks when analysing capital allocation.

ADE-045.q: A subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE) in a dynamic game is found by:
o: Backward induction from the end of the game
ADE-045.x:
Basis: Selten (1965, 1975) – subgame perfect equilibrium (Nobel 1994).
Analysis: Dynamic games of perfect information are solved by backward induction – start at the last decision node, choose the optimal action, substitute payoffs into earlier nodes, and move back to the start. SPE removes Nash equilibria resting on non-credible threats (ADE-047) – requiring optimal play in every subgame.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the method.

ADE-046.q: Entry game: an entrant chooses Enter or Stay out. Stay out: (incumbent 5, entrant 0). If it enters, the incumbent chooses Fight (−1, −1) or Accommodate (2, 1). What is the incumbent's SPE payoff?
ADE-046.e: After entry the incumbent accommodates (2 > −1); anticipating this the entrant enters (1 > 0) → incumbent gets 2.
ADE-046.x:
Basis: Game theory (entry game – Selten 1978 'chain-store paradox').
Working: Backward induction: if the entrant enters, the incumbent compares Fight −1 with Accommodate 2 → accommodates. Knowing this, the entrant gets 1 by entering > 0 staying out → enters. SPE: (Enter, Accommodate) → the incumbent gets 2.
Analysis: The incumbent loses 3 versus no entry (5), but fighting is worse (−1).

ADE-047.q: Entry game: an entrant chooses Enter or Stay out. Stay out: (incumbent 5, entrant 0). If it enters, the incumbent chooses Fight (−1, −1) or Accommodate (2, 1). The incumbent's threat 'I'll fight if you enter' is:
ADE-047.e: A threat is credible only with a commitment that changes payoffs (e.g., prior capacity investment).
o: Not credible, since once entry occurs fighting isn't optimal
ADE-047.x:
Basis: Game theory (credible threats – Schelling 1960; Dixit 1980 – capacity investment to deter entry).
Analysis: The 'we'll fight' threat isn't credible: once entry happens, fighting (−1) is worse than accommodating (2) → the incumbent won't carry it out → the entrant ignores it (ADE-046). Threats become credible only with prior commitments changing payoffs – e.g., large irreversible capacity investment making fighting optimal (ADE-056).
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.

ADE-048.q: By the folk theorem, in infinitely repeated games cooperation can be sustained if players value the future enough (high discount factor).
ADE-048.e: True. Punishment strategies (grim trigger, tit-for-tat) make defection unprofitable.
ADE-048.x:
Basis: Folk theorem (Friedman 1971; Fudenberg & Maskin 1986).
Analysis: True. In infinitely repeated games, if players value the future enough (high δ), any outcome giving each more than their minmax payoff can be sustained – including cooperation – via punishment strategies (grim trigger, tit-for-tat): a one-off gain from cheating is smaller than the endless punishment (ADE-049).
Note: It explains reputation-based long-term supplier and customer relationships.

ADE-049.q: Infinitely repeated game with grim trigger: cooperating yields 10 per period; defecting yields 15 once then 5 forever. What minimum discount factor δ sustains cooperation?
ADE-049.x:
Basis: Repeated game theory (grim trigger).
Working: Cooperate forever: 10 + 10δ + 10δ² + … = 10/(1 − δ). Defect: 15 + 5δ + 5δ² + … = 15 + 5δ/(1 − δ). Condition: 10/(1 − δ) ≥ 15 + 5δ/(1 − δ) → multiply by (1 − δ): 10 ≥ 15(1 − δ) + 5δ = 15 − 10δ → 10δ ≥ 5 → δ ≥ 0.5.
Check: δ = 0.5: cooperation 20; defection 15 + 5 = 20 → indifferent ✓.
Analysis: General formula: δ ≥ (temptation − cooperation) / (temptation − punishment) = (15 − 10)/(15 − 5) = 0.5.

o: Each player randomises so the opponent is indifferent among their choices
Each always plays one fixed strategy
ADE-050.x:
Basis: Nash (1950); von Neumann (1928) – mixed strategies.
Analysis: Mixed equilibrium: each player randomises so the opponent is indifferent between their pure strategies (otherwise the opponent would pick one and exploit it) – ADE-051. E.g., penalty kicks: kicker and keeper randomise left/right to stay unpredictable.
Distractors: B describes pure strategies; C – Nash's theorem guarantees at least one equilibrium in finite games (possibly mixed); D is wrong.

ADE-051.q: Column's payoffs: (Up, Left) = 2; (Down, Left) = 0; (Up, Right) = 0; (Down, Right) = 1. In the mixed equilibrium, with what probability does Row play Up (%, 2 decimals)?
ADE-051.x:
Basis: Game theory (mixed equilibrium – indifference principle).
Working: Let p = probability Row plays 'Up'. Column's expected payoff: Left = 2p + 0(1 − p) = 2p; Right = 0 × p + 1 × (1 − p) = 1 − p. Indifference: 2p = 1 − p → p = 1/3 ≈ 33.33%.
Check: 2 × 1/3 = 0.667 = 1 − 1/3 ✓.
Analysis: Row's probability comes from Column's payoffs (not Row's own) – a common mistake.

ADE-052.q: In a sealed-bid second-price (Vickrey) auction, the dominant strategy is to:
ADE-052.e: The price paid is set by the second-highest bid, so truthful bidding never hurts.
ADE-052.x:
Basis: Vickrey (1961), 'Counterspeculation, Auctions, and Competitive Sealed Tenders' (Nobel 1996).
Analysis: Second-price sealed bid: the top bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid. Bidding one's true value is dominant: underbidding risks losing a profitable win; overbidding risks winning at a price above value (a loss); the price paid doesn't depend on one's own bid → truth-telling never hurts.
Distractors: B and C are weakly worse; D is wrong.

ADE-053.q: Revenue equivalence: under standard assumptions (independent private values, risk neutrality), first- and second-price auctions yield the same expected revenue.
ADE-053.e: True. In practice they differ when assumptions fail (risk aversion, correlated values).
ADE-053.x:
Basis: Myerson (1981); Riley & Samuelson (1981) – revenue equivalence theorem.
Analysis: True. With independent private values, risk-neutral symmetric bidders and the highest-value bidder winning: first-price (bidders shade below value) and second-price (bid value, pay the second price) auctions yield the same expected revenue. Results differ when assumptions fail: risk-averse bidders → first-price earns more; correlated values → open and second-price formats do better.

ADE-054.e: Bidders should shade bids below their own estimates.
o: Common-value auctions (e.g., mining rights), where the winner tends to have the most optimistic estimate
ADE-054.x:
Basis: Capen, Clapp & Campbell (1971) – the winner's curse in oil-lease bidding; Thaler (1988).
Analysis: Common-value auctions (the true value is the same for all but unknown – mine reserves): each bidder's estimate has error; the winner is usually the most optimistic → overpaying relative to true value. Shade bids below your estimate, more so with more bidders.
Distractors: B – private values don't produce this curse; C and D are wrong.
Note (investing): buying 'hot' auctioned IPOs or paying up in acquisitions carries winner's-curse risk.

ADE-055.q: Second-price sealed-bid auction with bids 100, 120 and 90. What does the winner pay?
ADE-055.e: The 120 bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid = 100.
ADE-055.x:
Basis: Auction theory (Vickrey).
Working: Bids: 120 (highest – wins), 100 (second), 90. The winner pays the second-highest bid = 100.
Analysis: The winner's surplus = true value (120 if bidding truthfully) − 100 = 20. That's why truthful bidding is dominant (ADE-052).

ADE-056.q: Select ALL ways to create credible commitment in strategic competition:
ADE-056.e: Paradoxically, less flexibility can increase strategic power (Schelling).
o: Public commitments that damage reputation if broken
Keeping all options open to avoid commitment
ADE-056.x:
Basis: Schelling (1960) – The Strategy of Conflict; Dixit (1980).
Analysis: Credible commitments: (A) large, irreversible capacity investment upfront – making fighting optimal if a rival enters (ADE-047); (B) contracts with penalty clauses; (C) reputation from consistent action (repeated games – ADE-048); (D) public pledges that hurt credibility if broken.
Distractors: (E) Keeping every option open makes threats non-credible – Schelling's paradox: less flexibility can mean more strategic power ('burning bridges').
Note (investment discipline): pre-written rules and pre-set stops are commitments to oneself – guarding against mid-game system changes.

ADE-057.q: In Rubinstein's alternating-offers bargaining, who usually gets the larger share?
ADE-057.e: A first-mover advantage exists too but shrinks as waiting costs fall.
o: The more patient side (lower cost of waiting)
ADE-057.x:
Basis: Rubinstein (1982), 'Perfect Equilibrium in a Bargaining Model'.
Analysis: Alternating-offer bargaining with waiting costs (discounting): the more patient side (higher discount factor, lower waiting cost) gets more because its threat to wait is more credible. The first proposer's share = (1 − δ₂)/(1 − δ₁δ₂); the first-mover advantage shrinks as waiting costs fall.
Distractors: B is the reverse; C is wrong; D holds only for identical parties as waiting costs approach zero.
Note: In deals (M&A, property), the side under time pressure (needing liquidity, facing margin calls) is weaker.

ADE-058.q: Limit pricing to deter entry makes sense in a model with:
ADE-058.e: With perfect information, pre-entry prices don't affect entry (Milgrom–Roberts).
o: Asymmetric information: a low price signals the incumbent's low costs
Perfect information where entrants know costs
ADE-058.x:
Basis: Milgrom & Roberts (1982), 'Limit Pricing and Entry under Incomplete Information'.
Analysis: Bain (1949) argued low pre-entry prices deter entrants; but with perfect information the entrant knows the incumbent's costs, and pre-entry prices don't affect entry (only post-entry competition matters – ADE-046). Limit pricing makes sense with asymmetric information: low prices signal low costs → the entrant expects fierce post-entry competition → stays out.
Distractors: B, C and D can't explain it.

ADE-059.q: The Prospect Theory value function is:
ADE-059.e: It explains risk aversion for gains and risk seeking for losses.
o: Concave for gains, convex for losses, steeper for losses, defined relative to a reference point
ADE-059.x:
Basis: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) – Prospect theory (Nobel 2002).
Analysis: The value function: (1) measured relative to a reference point (gains/losses versus status quo, purchase price…), not total wealth; (2) concave for gains → risk-averse with gains (early profit-taking); (3) convex for losses → risk-seeking with losses (holding losers, 'getting even'); (4) steeper for losses → loss aversion (λ ≈ 2 – BAN-080, ADE-068).
Distractors: B, C and D describe standard expected utility or are wrong.
Note: It explains the disposition effect – 'taking profits too early' and 'holding because of cost'.

ADE-060.e: Commitment devices (automatic saving, locked accounts) help.
o: Procrastinating on saving or exercise despite plans – time-inconsistent preferences
ADE-060.x:
Basis: Laibson (1997), 'Golden Eggs and Hyperbolic Discounting'; O'Donoghue & Rabin (1999).
Analysis: Hyperbolic discounting: very high discount rates for near trade-offs (today versus tomorrow) but low for distant ones (year 10 versus 11) → time-inconsistent preferences: today we plan to save or exercise from next month; next month we postpone again. Commitment devices: automatic saving, locked accounts, public goals.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note: Relevant to personal discipline (sleep, meditation, less social media) and long-term investing – design environments and habits rather than relying on willpower.

ADE-061.q: Quasi-hyperbolic β–δ model with β = 0.7, δ = 0.95. What is the perceived present value of 100 received next period?
ADE-061.x:
Basis: Laibson (1997) – the quasi-hyperbolic β–δ model.
Working: Perceived present value of 100 next period = β × δ × 100 = 0.7 × 0.95 × 100 = 66.5 (without present bias: δ × 100 = 95).
Analysis: β = 0.7 is a blanket 'penalty' on all future amounts versus now → between periods 1 and 2 the discount is only δ = 0.95, but between today and period 1 it's 0.665 → strong present bias.
Check: 66.5 / 95 = 0.7 = β ✓.

ADE-062.q: 'Mental accounting' is the tendency to treat money differently by source or label, although money is fungible.
ADE-062.e: True (Thaler). E.g., spending bonuses more freely than salary.
ADE-062.x:
Basis: Thaler (1985), 'Mental Accounting and Consumer Choice'; Thaler (1999).
Analysis: True. Mental accounting: putting money into mental 'accounts' by source or purpose and treating them differently although money is fungible – bonuses and stock gains get spent more freely than salary; 'house money' (existing gains) gets gambled more.
Note (investing): judging holdings one by one (mental accounts) rather than as a portfolio leads to selling winners and keeping losers – evaluate the whole portfolio and opportunity costs.

ADE-063.e: It's linked to loss aversion: giving up the item feels like a loss.
o: The price to sell an owned item exceeds the price one would pay to buy it
Buy and sell prices are always equal
ADE-063.x:
Basis: Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler (1990), 'Experimental Tests of the Endowment Effect and the Coase Theorem'.
Analysis: The endowment effect: the price to sell something you own (WTA) is markedly higher than what you'd pay to buy it (WTP) – the mug experiments: WTA about twice WTP. It ties to loss aversion: giving it up feels like a loss (BAN-080).
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note (investing): valuing held stocks above similar unowned ones – test: 'If I didn't own it, would I buy at today's price?'.

ADE-064.e: Nudges preserve choice; bans aren't nudges.
o: Social norm messages ('80% of neighbours paid tax on time')
ADE-064.x:
Basis: Thaler & Sunstein (2008) – Nudge; the UK Behavioural Insights Team.
Analysis: A nudge alters choice architecture to steer behaviour predictably without banning options or significantly changing economic incentives: (A) beneficial defaults (BAN-087); (B) simpler procedures and forms; (C) timely reminders; (D) social-norm messages (UK tax-letter trials raised on-time payment).
Distractors: (E) An outright ban is a mandate, not a nudge – nudges preserve freedom of choice.

o: Very low offers (below about 20–30%) are often rejected though something beats nothing – people value fairness
ADE-065.x:
Basis: Güth, Schmittberger & Schwarze (1982) – the ultimatum game; Camerer (2003) – Behavioral Game Theory.
Analysis: Pure self-interest predicts the proposer offers the minimum and the responder accepts any positive amount. Experiments: offers of 40–50% are common; offers below about 20–30% are often rejected though something beats nothing → people value fairness and will pay to punish unfairness.
Distractors: B, C and D contradict the evidence.
Note: Relevant to negotiation and pay policy – perceived fairness affects cooperation.

ADE-066.q: Per Herbert Simon, due to limited information and processing capacity, people often choose 'good enough' options (satisficing) rather than optimal ones.
ADE-066.x:
Basis: Simon (1955), 'A Behavioral Model of Rational Choice' (Nobel 1978).
Analysis: True. Bounded rationality: limited information, time and computing ability → people can't optimise every choice → they use rules of thumb and pick 'good enough' options (satisficing) that meet aspiration levels.
Note (investment systems): screens with clear thresholds (P/E < 15, ROE > 15%…) are deliberate satisficing – simpler and easier to follow than complex optimisers.

ADE-067.q: People buying both lottery tickets and insurance is explained in Prospect Theory by:
ADE-067.e: The probability weighting function inflates small probabilities.
ADE-067.x:
Basis: Kahneman & Tversky (1979); Tversky & Kahneman (1992) – probability weighting.
Analysis: The weighting function inflates small probabilities (and deflates moderate–high ones) → people overrate lottery wins (buying despite negative EV) and catastrophes (insuring small risks) → doing both at once, contradicting standard expected utility (consistent risk aversion or seeking).
Distractors: B, C and D can't explain it.
Note (investing): a taste for 'lottery' stocks (penny stocks, hoped-for multibaggers) tends to deliver low average returns (Barberis & Huang 2008).

ADE-068.q: A loss-averse person with λ = 2 (linear value, no probability weighting) considers a 50% win 100 / 50% lose 60 gamble. What is its perceived value?
ADE-068.x:
Basis: Prospect theory (λ – loss aversion coefficient).
Working: Perceived value = 0.5 × 100 − 0.5 × λ × 60 = 50 − 0.5 × 2 × 60 = 50 − 60 = −10 → reject. True expected value = 0.5 × 100 − 0.5 × 60 = +20.
Analysis: Loss aversion rejects a positive-EV gamble. Samuelson (1963): someone rejecting one bet may accept a series – narrow framing leads to rejecting small favourable risks.
Note: Checking a portfolio too often shows more losses → myopic loss aversion (Benartzi & Thaler 1995) – linked to over-monitoring.

ADE-069.e: It can be individually rational (following others' signals) yet destabilising overall.
o: Amplify asset bubbles and crashes, pushing prices far from fundamentals
ADE-069.x:
Basis: Banerjee (1992), Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer & Welch (1992) – information cascades; Shiller – Irrational Exuberance.
Analysis: Herding: investors follow the crowd or others' signals (individually rational when private information is weak – cascades) → prices drift far from fundamentals, amplifying bubbles on the way up and crashes on reversal, raising volatility.
Distractors: B, C and D say the opposite.
Note (psychology – FOMO): this is the FOMO mechanism; valuation discipline and separated deployment rules (the 'separation of powers') counter herding.

ADE-070.q: Behavioural economics completely rejects standard economics.
ADE-070.e: False. It adds psychological realism to better describe actual behaviour.
ADE-070.x:
Basis: Behavioural economics (Thaler 2015 – Misbehaving; Rabin 1998).
Analysis: False. Behavioural economics complements rather than rejects standard economics: it keeps the framework (optimisation, equilibrium) and adds empirically tested psychology (biases, bounded rationality, social preferences) to describe and predict real behaviour better. Standard models remain the normative benchmark (how one should behave).

ADE-071.q: The Solow steady state (no technological progress) satisfies:
ADE-071.e: Investment exactly offsets depreciation and population growth.
ADE-071.x:
Basis: Solow (1956) – steady state.
Analysis: Capital per worker changes: Δk = s·f(k) − (n + δ)k. Steady state at Δk = 0 → s·f(k) = (n + δ)k: investment (saving) just covers depreciation (δk) and equips new workers (nk). With technology growth g: s·f(k) = (n + δ + g)k (k per effective worker).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the condition.

ADE-072.q: Solow model: y = √k, saving rate s = 0.2, n + δ = 0.05. What is steady-state capital per worker k*?
ADE-072.x:
Basis: Solow (1956).
Working: s·√k = (n + δ)k → 0.2√k = 0.05k → 0.2 = 0.05√k → √k = 4 → k* = 16.
Check: Investment 0.2 × √16 = 0.8 = depreciation plus dilution 0.05 × 16 = 0.8 ✓.
General formula with y = k^α: k* = (s/(n + δ))^(1/(1−α)) = (0.2/0.05)² = 16 ✓.

ADE-073.q: Solow model: y = √k, saving rate s = 0.2, n + δ = 0.05. What is steady-state output per worker y*?
ADE-073.x:
Basis: Solow (1956).
Working: y* = √k* = √16 = 4.
Analysis: With y = k^α: y* = (s/(n + δ))^(α/(1−α)) = 4^1 = 4 ✓. Raising s to 0.3 → k* = 36, y* = 6 – a level effect, not a change in long-run growth (MCR-094).

ADE-074.q: Solow model: y = √k, saving rate s = 0.2, n + δ = 0.05. What is steady-state consumption per worker c*?
ADE-074.x:
Basis: Solow (1956).
Working: c* = (1 − s) × y* = (1 − 0.2) × 4 = 3.2.
Analysis: Consumption = output − investment = 4 − 0.8 = 3.2 ✓. Versus the golden rule (s = 50% – ADE-076): k = 100, y = 10, c = 5 > 3.2 → the economy saves below the golden rule; saving more would raise long-run consumption (though cutting it during transition).

ADE-075.q: The golden-rule capital level maximising steady-state consumption satisfies:
ADE-075.e: Over-saving (k above golden rule) lowers consumption – dynamic inefficiency.
o: Marginal product of capital equals n + δ
ADE-075.x:
Basis: Phelps (1961), 'The Golden Rule of Accumulation'.
Analysis: Steady-state consumption c* = f(k*) − (n + δ)k* → maximised where the derivative in k is zero: f'(k) = n + δ – the marginal product of capital equals depreciation plus population growth. If k exceeds the golden-rule level (over-saving – dynamic inefficiency), cutting saving raises consumption at all dates.
Distractors: B means zero consumption; C doesn't maximise consumption; D holds only if n + δ = 0.

ADE-076.q: With y = √k and n + δ = 0.05, what is the golden-rule saving rate (%)?
ADE-076.e: MPK = 0.5/√k = 0.05 → √k = 10 → k = 100, y = 10; s = (n + δ)k/y = 0.05 × 100/10 = 50% (equal to capital's Cobb–Douglas share).
ADE-076.x:
Basis: Phelps (1961).
Working: MPK = d√k/dk = 0.5/√k = n + δ = 0.05 → √k = 10 → k_gold = 100; y = √100 = 10; s_gold = (n + δ)k / y = 0.05 × 100 / 10 = 50%.
Check: c = 10 − 5 = 5, above the 3.2 at s = 20% (ADE-074) ✓.
Analysis: With Cobb–Douglas y = k^α, s_gold = α = 0.5 – capital's income share.

ADE-077.q: In an AK endogenous growth model, a higher saving rate can raise the long-run growth rate.
ADE-077.e: True. There are no diminishing returns to (broad) capital including human capital and knowledge.
ADE-077.x:
Basis: Rebelo (1991) – the AK model; Romer (1986), Lucas (1988) – endogenous growth.
Analysis: True. AK model: Y = AK, with broad capital (physical, human, knowledge) facing no diminishing returns → growth g = sA − δ (ADE-078) → higher saving/investment permanently raises long-run growth – unlike Solow (level effect only – MCR-094). Implication: policies encouraging education and R&D affect long-run growth.

ADE-078.q: AK model: g = sA − δ with s = 0.25, A = 0.4, δ = 0.05. What is long-run growth (%)?
ADE-078.x:
Basis: AK model.
Working: g = sA − δ = 0.25 × 0.4 − 0.05 = 0.10 − 0.05 = 0.05 = 5%.
Analysis: Raising s to 0.3 → g = 0.12 − 0.05 = 7% – permanently higher growth (ADE-077). Higher capital productivity A (investment efficiency) also lifts growth – linked to a low ICOR (MCR-099, ICOR ≈ 1/A).

ADE-079.q: Per Romer, ideas drive sustained growth because:
ADE-079.e: IP protection and market size shape innovation incentives.
o: Ideas are non-rival, creating increasing returns to scale
Only one person can use an idea
ADE-079.x:
Basis: Romer (1990), 'Endogenous Technological Change' (Nobel 2018).
Analysis: Ideas are non-rival (one formula or program serves countless users at once with low copying cost) → increasing returns to scale – new ideas raise productivity economy-wide without the diminishing returns of physical capital → sustained growth. Partial excludability (patents) motivates innovation; larger markets raise its payoff.
Distractors: B, C and D misstate the nature.

ADE-080.q: The human-capital-augmented Solow model (Mankiw–Romer–Weil) explains cross-country income gaps better because it:
ADE-080.e: A higher 'broad' capital share slows convergence, matching data.
o: Adds investment in education and skills alongside physical capital
ADE-080.x:
Basis: Mankiw, Romer & Weil (1992), 'A Contribution to the Empirics of Economic Growth'.
Analysis: Adding human capital (education, skills investment) to the Solow production function → explaining about 80% of cross-country income differences (versus about 60% with basic Solow). A higher 'broad' capital share (physical + human ≈ 2/3) → slower convergence (≈ 2% a year), matching the data.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.

ADE-081.q: Per Acemoglu–Robinson, select ALL features of growth-promoting 'inclusive' institutions:
ADE-081.e: High inflation distorts price signals and cuts investment.
o: Rule of law and contract enforcement
ADE-081.x:
Basis: Acemoglu & Robinson (2012) – Why Nations Fail (Nobel 2024 with Johnson).
Analysis: Inclusive economic institutions: (A) secure property rights; (B) rule of law and contract enforcement; (C) constraints on executive power (pluralistic politics); (D) broad economic participation and fair competition → encouraging investment, innovation and 'creative destruction' (ADE-084). Extractive institutions serve a narrow elite and stunt long-run growth.
Distractors: (E) Persistent high inflation distorts price signals and cuts investment.

ADE-082.q: Real GDP grows 6.5% and population 0.9%. What is approximate per-capita GDP growth (%)?
ADE-082.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (per-capita growth).
Working: Approximation: 6.5% − 0.9% = 5.6%. Exact: 1.065 / 1.009 − 1 ≈ 5.55%.
Analysis: Living standards depend on per-capita, not total, GDP growth. As Vietnam ages, population and labour growth slow → growth must rely more on productivity (MCR-091, MCR-096).

ADE-083.q: In the Solow model, capital accumulation alone (no technological progress) can sustain per-capita income growth forever.
ADE-083.e: False. Diminishing returns drive the economy to a steady state.
ADE-083.x:
Basis: Solow (1956).
Analysis: False. Without technological progress, capital accumulation faces diminishing returns: as k rises, extra output per unit of capital falls while depreciation and dilution grow linearly → the economy converges to the steady state k* (ADE-072), and per-capita income stops growing. Long-run per-capita growth comes only from technology (MCR-094).

ADE-084.e: The Aghion–Howitt model formalises this idea.
o: Innovation replacing old technologies and firms, generating growth with disruption
ADE-084.x:
Basis: Schumpeter (1942) – Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy; Aghion & Howitt (1992).
Analysis: Creative destruction: innovation (new technologies, products, business models) displaces old technologies and firms – driving productivity growth but causing disruption (closures, job losses). Aghion–Howitt formalised it: growth via a sequence of quality-improving innovations, each replacing the previous innovator's temporary monopoly.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the concept.
Note (investing): moats can be broken by innovation – assess substitution-technology risk when judging moat durability.

ADE-085.q: An estimated regression is Ŷ = 2 + 0.5X. The correct interpretation of 0.5:
ADE-085.e: A causal reading needs exogeneity assumptions.
o: A 1-unit rise in X is associated with a 0.5-unit average rise in Y (holding other model variables fixed)
ADE-085.x:
Basis: Wooldridge – Introductory Econometrics (interpreting coefficients).
Analysis: A coefficient of 0.5: a one-unit rise in X raises Y by 0.5 on average, other model factors held constant (ceteris paribus in multiple regression). A causal reading needs exogeneity E(u|X) = 0 – no omitted variables, reverse causality or measurement error (ADE-089).
Distractors: B is a log-model reading; C – correlation ≠ causation (ADE-088); D – 2 is Y at X = 0 (the intercept).

ADE-086.q: With Ŷ = 2 + 0.5X, what is predicted Y at X = 10?
ADE-086.x:
Basis: Wooldridge – Econometrics (prediction).
Working: Ŷ = 2 + 0.5 × 10 = 2 + 5 = 7.
Analysis: Predictions within the estimation data's range (interpolation) are more reliable than far extrapolation. Report a prediction interval reflecting error, not just the point.

ADE-087.e: High R² proves neither causality nor correct specification.
o: 65% of the variation in the dependent variable is explained by the model's regressors
ADE-087.x:
Basis: Wooldridge – Econometrics (R²).
Analysis: R² = 0.65: 65% of the dependent variable's variation (sum of squared deviations) around its mean is explained by the model's variables; 35% is residual. A high R² proves neither causality nor model correctness (it may be spurious – ADE-099), and R² always rises with more variables (use adjusted R²) → overfitting risk (ADE-100).
Distractors: B, C and D misinterpret it.

ADE-088.q: A strong correlation between two variables proves one causes the other.
ADE-088.e: False. It may reflect a third variable, reverse causality or chance.
ADE-088.x:
Basis: Econometrics; Pearl (2009) – Causality.
Analysis: False. Strong correlation may come from: a confounder (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer); reverse causality (Y causes X); coincidence, especially with trending time series (ADE-099). Establishing causality needs research design: RCTs (ADE-092), instruments (ADE-090), DiD (ADE-091), RDD (ADE-097).
Note (investing): historical correlations between indicators and prices (e.g., MACD signals and returns) need a mechanism and out-of-sample tests before becoming rules.

ADE-089.q: Regressing wages on years of schooling while omitting 'ability' (positively correlated with both), the schooling coefficient will be:
ADE-089.e: Omitted variable bias = the omitted variable's effect × its correlation with the regressor.
ADE-089.x:
Basis: Wooldridge – Econometrics (omitted variable bias); Griliches (1977) – ability and returns to schooling.
Analysis: Omitted variable bias = β_ability × the (regression) coefficient of ability on schooling. Ability raises wages (β > 0) and correlates positively with schooling → positive bias → the schooling coefficient is overstated (absorbing ability's effect).
Distractors: B – downward bias needs opposite signs; C – there is bias; D is wrong.

ADE-090.e: Weak instruments give biased, unreliable estimates.
o: Correlate with the endogenous regressor (relevance) and affect the outcome only through it (exclusion)
ADE-090.x:
Basis: Angrist & Pischke (2009) – Mostly Harmless Econometrics; Angrist & Krueger (1991).
Analysis: A valid instrument Z: (1) relevance – Z correlates with the endogenous X (testable via the first stage, F > 10 as a rule of thumb); (2) exclusion – Z affects Y only through X, uncorrelated with the error (not directly testable; needs argument). Weak instruments bias estimates toward OLS and make inference unreliable.
Distractors: B violates exclusion; C – an unrelated variable does nothing; D – lagged dependents often fail with autocorrelation.

ADE-091.q: Difference-in-differences: the treated group's revenue goes from 10 to 18; the control from 9 to 13. What is the estimated policy effect?
ADE-091.x:
Basis: Angrist & Pischke; Card & Krueger (1994) – the New Jersey minimum wage study.
Working: DiD = (after − before)_treated − (after − before)_control = (18 − 10) − (13 − 9) = 8 − 4 = 4.
Analysis: The control group shows what would have happened without the policy (a common +4 trend); the extra 4 is the policy effect. Key assumption: parallel trends – check with several pre-policy periods.

ADE-092.q: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard because:
o: Random assignment balances confounders (observed and unobserved) across groups
ADE-092.x:
Basis: Angrist & Pischke; Banerjee & Duflo (Nobel 2019) – RCTs in development economics.
Analysis: RCTs are the gold standard because random assignment balances confounders – observed and unobserved – (in expectation) across treatment and control → outcome differences are causal effects. Limits: external validity (results may not transfer), cost, ethics, Hawthorne effects.
Distractors: B – samples needn't be large; C – statistics are still needed; D – generalisability is a limitation.

ADE-093.q: An estimated coefficient is 0.6 with standard error 0.2. What is the t-statistic?
ADE-093.x:
Basis: Wooldridge – Econometrics (t-test).
Working: t = coefficient / standard error = 0.6 / 0.2 = 3.
Analysis: |t| = 3 > 1.96 (5% critical value, large sample) → reject H₀: coefficient = 0 → statistically significant (p ≈ 0.003). 95% CI ≈ 0.6 ± 1.96 × 0.2 = [0.21; 0.99]. Economic significance still needs assessment (ADE-095).

ADE-094.q: A p-value of 0.03 when testing H₀: coefficient = 0. The correct interpretation:
ADE-094.e: A p-value isn't the probability the hypothesis is true.
o: If H₀ were true, the chance of a result at least this extreme is 3%; reject H₀ at the 5% level
ADE-094.x:
Basis: Statistics; ASA Statement on p-values (Wasserstein & Lazar 2016).
Analysis: p = 0.03: if H₀ were true, results this extreme or more would occur 3% of the time → reject H₀ at 5% (not at 1%). The p-value isn't the probability H₀ is true, nor a measure of effect size or importance; p < 0.05 isn't a true/false line.
Distractors: B is the most common misreading; C and D are wrong.

ADE-095.q: A statistically significant result is always economically important.
ADE-095.e: False. With huge samples, tiny effects are significant; magnitude matters.
ADE-095.x:
Basis: Statistics (McCloskey & Ziliak 1996 – statistical versus economic significance).
Analysis: False. With huge samples, standard errors are tiny → trivial effects (e.g., a policy lifting revenue 0.01%) become statistically significant but economically unimportant. Conversely, large effects may be insignificant in small samples. Report magnitudes and confidence intervals and judge in context.
Note (backtests): a 'statistically significant' excess return smaller than trading costs and taxes has no practical value.

ADE-096.q: Select ALL issues to check when using OLS on economic data:
ADE-096.e: OLS doesn't require an integer dependent variable.
o: The dependent variable must be an integer
ADE-096.x:
Basis: Wooldridge – Econometrics (Gauss–Markov assumptions).
Analysis: Check: (A) heteroskedasticity – use robust (White, HC) standard errors; (B) multicollinearity – inflating standard errors and destabilising coefficients (VIF); (C) serial correlation in time series – use Newey–West or dynamic models; (D) endogeneity – regressors correlated with errors (omitted variables, reverse causality, measurement error) → bias, needing IV (ADE-090).
Distractors: (E) OLS doesn't require an integer dependent variable (count models like Poisson exist but aren't mandatory).

ADE-097.q: Regression discontinuity design (RDD) suits cases where:
ADE-097.e: It compares units just above and below the cutoff as if randomly assigned.
o: Treatment depends on a threshold of a continuous variable (e.g., score ≥ 25 earns a scholarship)
Data are a single cross-section without thresholds
ADE-097.x:
Basis: Thistlethwaite & Campbell (1960); Lee & Lemieux (2010) – regression discontinuity.
Analysis: RDD fits when treatment is set by a threshold in a continuous variable (exam score ≥ 25 for a scholarship, revenue below a tax-incentive cutoff, a 51% ownership line). Comparing units just above and below – as good as random → the jump in outcomes at the threshold is a local causal effect. Check for manipulation of the running variable around the cutoff.
Distractors: B calls for an RCT; C – a threshold is required; D – a binary outcome isn't the condition.

ADE-098.q: Log–log model: ln(spending) = a + 0.8 × ln(income). If income rises 10%, by roughly how much does spending rise (%)?
ADE-098.e: In a log–log model the coefficient is an elasticity: 0.8 × 10% = 8%.
ADE-098.x:
Basis: Wooldridge – Econometrics (log–log model).
Working: The log–log coefficient is an elasticity: %ΔSpending ≈ 0.8 × 10% = 8%. Exact: 1.1^0.8 − 1 ≈ 7.92%.
Analysis: An income elasticity of spending of 0.8 < 1 → spending grows slower than income → saving rates rise with income (consistent with Keynes's falling MPC). Same logic as BAN-072 (price elasticity).

ADE-099.q: Regressing two trending (non-stationary) series like GDP and house prices gives a very high R². The main risk is:
ADE-099.e: Two series rising over time may correlate though unrelated.
o: Spurious regression; test for unit roots, cointegration or difference the data
ADE-099.x:
Basis: Granger & Newbold (1974), 'Spurious Regressions in Econometrics'; Engle & Granger (1987) – cointegration.
Analysis: Regressing two trending non-stationary series (GDP, house prices, stock indices) on each other often yields high R² and large t-stats with no real relation – spurious regression (sign: Durbin–Watson very low, below R²). Remedies: unit-root tests (ADF, KPSS); difference non-stationary series (growth rates), or test cointegration (Engle–Granger, Johansen) if a genuine long-run link exists.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note (investing): test correlations between two stocks/indices on returns (differences), not price levels.

ADE-100.q: A many-variable forecasting model fits history very well but forecasts poorly. Likely cause and fix:
ADE-100.e: This applies to trading strategies and credit scoring too.
o: Overfitting; out-of-sample testing, simpler models, cross-validation
ADE-100.x:
Basis: Applied statistics (Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman – Elements of Statistical Learning); Bailey & López de Prado (2014) – backtest overfitting.
Analysis: A many-variable, many-parameter model that fits history well but forecasts poorly → overfitting: it learned the noise. Remedies: out-of-sample (walk-forward) tests, cross-validation, simplification (fewer parameters, regularisation), information criteria (AIC/BIC), limiting the number of trials (data snooping).
Distractors: B, C and D are the opposite.
Note (TradingView/FERGASITOR): optimising MACD or Supertrend parameters on one period and declaring victory is overfitting – forward-test across regimes and different tickers; fewer parameters are sturdier and easier to follow.
